title: ‘I can’t show my true self too much on LinkedIn’: This 17-year-old AI founder networked his way all the way to the United Nations
summary: Rhythm Bazari, a high school senior, says all of his networking opportunities have come through the platform. "I can't show my true self too much."
content: Rhythm Bazari, a high school senior in Atlanta, says every networking opportunity he has had came through LinkedIn, including his invitation to speak at United Nations events during high-level week in September. He also says the person who writes on the platform isn’t quite the person he is in real life. “Every networking thing I’ve done has been through LinkedIn, to be honest,” said Bazari, 17. “I wouldn’t have found out about a lot of stuff if it wasn’t for LinkedIn.” Earlier this month, LinkedIn said the number of members listing “Founder” on their profiles has risen 125% since 2022, with new Gen Z businesses up 275%. Asked whether there is a LinkedIn Rhythm and a real one, he said, “I think so.” On the platform, he said, “I try to be more service lesson-oriented versus how I am in person.” He added: “I can’t show my true self too much on LinkedIn.” How he got in It started on Instagram. “I see these students who are my age, and I’m like, how are they getting to the United Nations? And I’m not going there,” Bazari said. He began researching and contacted a major UN youth organization, which didn’t respond at first. He then went through a third-party group, the International Organization of Youth, which pointed him to a flagship event near the UN. People he met there invited him to speak on the “AI and Human Development” panel. “It was very last minute,” he said. “When I got invited, it didn’t feel real, to be honest.” He spoke at a UN event on AI and human development that had no youth speakers, he said. His pitch: “We’re the generation who’s going to deal with AI the most.” That’s what his company, Avants AI, is about. It began as an AI community project and has evolved into an AI tool that vets job candidates. “Now we’re making an automated interview process,” he said, adding that he built it with KR3 Information Systems, a cybersecurity company where he has interned since ninth or tenth grade. Avants AI has about 1,000 users and has summarized 5,000 resumes, Bazari said. “We’re not making any money right now because we’re mainly in the product shipping stage,” he said. “It’s mainly for free right now.” An AI believer’s caveats Bazari’s product lands in a hiring market that is already automated. In a five-country Greenhouse survey of about 1,350 recruiters and hiring managers, 52% of employers said they already use AI interviews, and 73% use or plan to use them within a year. Northeastern University researchers found that 54% of U.S. hiring decision-makers use AI to screen resumes at least some of the time. Among those whose hiring AI has changed, 26% said they hire fewer entry-level workers because of it, against 7% who hire more. In the Greenhouse survey, 90% of U.S. employers said they may have turned away real candidates because applications looked fake or AI-generated. Bazari said his own research found that recruiters “spend six or seven seconds on your resume,” and they prefer to see real work over stats. His advice to job seekers: show the code base for what you built. “I feel like people are not understanding that AI can really automate everything,” Bazari said, adding that he worries about overreliance. “Whenever I pull up a package, I’m like, ‘Claude, just tell me what this does.’ I actively learn while it does everything for me.” Bazari said his team has submitted early college applications. He started posting on LinkedIn during his junior year, when it felt like “educational Instagram, a very mature Instagram.” He says he writes his own posts. “I try to keep my personal voice,” he said, and uses AI only for images. His motive, he said, is helping people. “I’m definitely trying to be impressive,” he said, “it’s part of the deal, I guess.” Still, he stressed, “the main focus is helping .” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

title: Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky says staff call him a ‘control freak’—but that he learned it from Apple’s Steve Jobs
summary: Aribnb's billionaire CEO Brian Chesky called Apple’s Steve Jobs a 'control freak,' before admitting Airbnb workers probably say the same about him.
content: Airbnb’s billionaire CEO Brian Chesky recently admitted that some of his workers probably call him a “control freak.” But he says he’s in good company, as he picked up the habit from studying Apple’s Steve Jobs. “People called him a control freak. He probably was a control freak,” Chesky told Time . “He held people to extremely high standards. He spent a lot of time recruiting. He was in the details.” When asked whether Airbnb staff would say the same, Chesky responded: “I think some people do.” He also spends 3 hours a day recruiting and tells his hiring managers to leave if they don’t like his input. But he insists that doesn’t mean he’s micromanaging his workforce—and he even talked to the man who worked closest to Jobs to prove it. Jony Ive worked with Steve Jobs for nearly 15 years—and said he wasn’t a micromanager Apple’s former design chief, Jony Ive, worked alongside the late cofounder for nearly 15 years in designing iconic products like the iMac, iPod, iPhone, iPad, and Apple Watch. And so Chesky once point-blank asked Ive what it was like working for Jobs. “Johny said to me, ‘I never felt like Steve was micromanaging,” Chesky recalled, adding that Ive’s felt like they were just “constantly partnering” because Jobs wasn’t outright telling him what to do. He just wanted to be in on the details. They’d even have lunch together every day . “Constantly working back and forth,” Chesky added. And that’s where the Airbnb boss draws the line. He said “micromanagement, where you’re like telling people what to do” is a last resort—and probably an indicator of how well they’re going to do at his company. “If I’m telling somebody what to do, they’re probably not successful,” Chesky added. “So the best thing is we’re partnering. I’m asking questions. What if we did this? What if we did that? Now I’m not doing that with my chief accounting officer, I’m not doing that with a tax attorney. I’m doing that in areas where I think it can add value, like product, marketing, operations, things like that.” Chesky has defended this idea before , arguing that “micromanagement” isn’t about control; it’s about helping people think bigger and move faster. In a previous interview, Chesky explained that being in the details shouldn’t diminish anyone’s autonomy or make your reports feel like the boss is hovering over their shoulder or undermining them. Instead, it should make them feel like their manager is invested in them. “So here’s the question: If I’m in the details with somebody, am I making them better or am I disempowering them? And I hope that when people feel like I’m involved in projects, they feel like I’m helping them push to think bigger,” he told CNBC . How Chesky micromanages his 7,300 Airbnb employees With over 9 million active listings in over 150,000 cities in 220 countries and over 8,200 employees , Chesky also argues that getting into the weeds is necessary to get things done swiftly. “There’s a paradox where being in the details sounds like micromanagement; it sounds like it’s slowing teams down,” the 45-year-old entrepreneur continued in the CNBC interview. “But when you’re in the details, you can actually help make decisions faster.” Essentially, layers of approval, endless meetings, and hours of wasted worker time can be saved when someone with real sign-off power is in the room. “The number of people in organizations that [have] to get through managers and managers and managers to approve something, but then all these leaders have to agree to something, there’s a bunch of meetings—peers can’t make fast decisions,” Chesky added. “Only a leader can make a quick decision in a room. I bring everyone in the room, everyone makes a recommendation, and we can make a really, really fast decision. “I think that’s the key of a leader, to make decisions,” he said. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

title: The pig in the python in the marital bed: How boomers deformed the Silent Generation’s marriages, Gen X’s childhood and millennials’ housing
summary: A new peer-reviewed paper finds the baby boom’s sheer size helped drive the 1970s divorce boom—“likely about a third at most,” its author says.
content: The baby boom has been called “the pig in the python” since at least 1974, when Russell Baker gave the 76 million-strong bulge its name by using the disturbing image of a python swallowing a pig and struggling to digest it, just the way the economy is struggling to digest the bulge of the largest generation in history. It’s becoming increasingly clear, as the baby boomers push the median age of the U.S. population toward 40, that the generation is so big that it has created its own markets as it moves through life. In the current economy, this market-making dynamic is most visible in housing , where empty-nest boomers own 28% of U.S. homes with three or more bedrooms, compared with 16% for millennial parents, according to a Redfin analysis of Census data. The first-time homebuyer age has jumped to match the record-high median age of 40, the National Association of Realtors found last November. A new peer-reviewed paper suggests the python bulge was being felt decades ago in the marriage market of the 1970s and the bonanza in divorces that resulted. In an article titled “ The baby boom and the US divorce boom ,” published this month in the European Economic Review , Tereza Ranošová, an economist at the Deutsche Bundesbank Research Center, argues that the two postwar booms, in births after 1945 and in divorces about 25 years later, are linked. The U.S. divorce rate more than doubled between 1960 and 1980. Ranošová’s explanation is mostly arithmetic. “As men typically match with younger women, a large young cohort presents a supply shock to the remarriage options of husbands in existing partnerships,” she writes in the paper. So when the boom’s huge cohorts reached marrying age, the men just ahead of them, mostly the Silent Generation, born just before and during World War II, faced an unusually large supply of younger women. Those young women, meanwhile, were short of single men their own age, “making it more worthwhile for young women to match with already married men,” she writes. While standard models assume singles only marry singles, Ranošová treats married men as still on the market: “When younger women are abundant, some divorce to rematch with them.” “These men had the most options among women somewhat younger than them (who in turn were desperate for options, so they settled for already married men),” Ranošová told Fortune in an email. The paper finds evidence that some of those marriages ended in divorce and remarriage. She’s careful about how much this explains. “I would not want to overstate here,” she said. “I would say likely about a third at most.” She sees the boom as a push that “brought people closer to the decision,” while shifting social norms made divorce possible. “Once the norm was broken, it would be hard to attribute things to specific causes.” A market, not a morality tale The paper’s evidence is a comparison across states. Using 1960 and 1980 Census data on more than 2.2 million people ages 35 to 44, Ranošová found that people born in states with a bigger early baby boom were more likely to have ever divorced. The link held when Ranošová used World War II mobilization rates, which earlier research ties to the size of each state’s boom, to make it less likely that those states simply had different family values. The U.S. divorce rate (dashed line, by year) and the share of men who ever divorced (red dots, by birth cohort) rose and fell together, both peaking around 1980. Tereza Ranošová, European Economic Review (CC BY 4.0) The squeeze cut both ways. Early boomer women found men a few years older scarce, Ranošová said. Some married men their own age; others married older men, more often ones who had been married before. The paper also raises, without settling, the possibility that no-fault divorce laws loosened in the 1970s partly because demand for divorce was already building. Betsy Cox isn’t just a boomer — and a divorcee — herself, she founded Blackbook, which led the way in creating the “ divorce concierge ” service for the ultrawealthy. She hadn’t read Ranošová’s research, or even thought of the angle, but said “I totally agree with that” when asked by Fortune . “It’s very true, very true,” she said, adding that the boomers were “probably one of the reasons I started Blackbook Divorce. She recalled being one of the first people in her cohort to get divorced and then she saw firsthand the boomer divorce effect take flight. “I was the first, but then it was, boom! It was like, oh my God, crazy. It was everybody.” Cox’s business has evolved away from a pure divorce concierge; she’s just launched Blackbook Circle, which she described as a “private service that gives successful men a straight answer from a woman who’s seen it all, and then a team that handles it.” A lot of her new business consists of what she calls “AI guys,” who she sees as “refreshing.” “They’re not full of themselves and I think they would make good husbands and boyfriends because they’re nice guys,” Cox said. At the same time, she “100%” sees a divorce wave coming in as the AI wealth transforms lives overnight. Many of them want the traditional trappings of wealth. “They move maybe from San Fran to New York, a few of them. They want to be in the Hamptons, and they want to be into the clubs,” she said. The boomers are making the reverse commute, Cox said. “Those baby boomers that are in New York are now leaving because there’s a lot of men and women that, first of all, they’re getting taxed heavily — if you say New York or LA, but there’s nothing left.” She added that coastal boomers “feel like they’ve done it all. They have enough money. They don’t have to worry. They just can’t find anybody, and that’s a whole other story of how it’s not pretty out there.” The boomer wave had a long tail, when you look at the marital outcomes of Gen X and millennials. Gen X, children of divorce Gen X icon Kurt Cobain rejected the label of being a spokesman for his generation with trademark irony, writing the lyric “that legendary divorce is such a bore.” Nevertheless, nearly every alternative rocker came from what was called a “broken home” in the 1970s, from Billy Corgan to Eddie Vedder to Dave Grohl. The great music podcaster Yasi Salek, of Bandsplain, has argued that Cobain’s grunge genre was the product of a whole generation of American men reeling from their parents’ divorces. The numbers behind them are broad. In 1960, 73% of American children lived with two parents in their first marriage. By 1980 it was 61%, according to Pew Research Center . Before 1950, fewer than 2% of children lived with a single parent who was divorced, separated or never married. By 2000, nearly 25% did, the Census Bureau reported . Still, the famous claim that half of all marriages end in divorce comes closest to true for the Gen X childhood decade. Economists Betsey Stevenson and Justin Wolfers found that 48% of marriages formed in the 1970s had dissolved within 25 years. That’s the decade the baby boom hit the marriage market and Gen X was growing up. The divorce rate peaked around 1980, and each marriage cohort since has done better. By 2024, the refined divorce rate was down to 14.2 per 1,000 married women, according to Bowling Green State University’s National Center for Family & Marriage Research . Ranošová ties much of the decline to people marrying less and later, which she said means “better matches in the first place.” What stuck from the 1970s was the norm. Divorce went from rare to ordinary and never went back. Andrew Cherlin, a Johns Hopkins sociologist who has studied divorce for decades, wrote in 2000 that the American divorce rate doubled in the 1960s and ’70s, with a million children a year going through a parental divorce. Ranošová was reluctant to tie her mechanism to Gen X’s own attitudes toward marriage. “I think that would be way too much extrapolation. I have no evidence on that,” she said. The long tail The generations at the center of the boom kept divorcing. Among Americans 50 and older, the divorce rate doubled from 5 per 1,000 married people in 1990 to 10 in 2015, Pew found . For those 65 and older, it roughly tripled. Remarriages are a big part of it. Over-50s in a second or later marriage divorced at twice the rate of those married once, and 48% of the over-50s who divorced in 2015 were in a remarriage. Ranošová called it “not implausible” that her cohorts show up in those numbers. Those born between 1935 and 1945 being more often divorced in later life than the generation before “matches the mechanism,” she said. That could reflect both the original mismatch and the fact that more of them are in higher-order marriages, which “are statistically more prone to divorce.” Still, she guessed much of it “has to do also with less social stigma and a different economic role marriage plays.” The money stakes are real: retirement accounts get split and the lower earner can lose Social Security income, Fortune has reported . The divorce boom’s longest legacy may be fewer marriages. That matters for more than the wedding industry. University of Chicago economist Sam Peltzman has spent years combing the General Social Survey, which has asked Americans since 1972 whether they’re happy. His measure, the share saying “very happy” minus the share saying “not very happy,” ran at roughly +20 points on average from 1972 through 2018, steady through wars and recessions. Then 2020 knocked it down 22.2 points, by far the largest single move in the survey’s history, and for the first time more Americans said they were not very happy than very happy. By 2024 it had come back only to around +6, he told Fortune in May . Peltzman called it a “regime change” and something of a happiness recession. The crash split the country along marriage lines. Married Americans have scored roughly 31 points higher on his scale than unmarried ones for 50 years, a “marital premium” that held across gender, race, age, income and education. After 2020, the married fell, too, but stayed comfortably positive. The unmarried, about 45% of adults 25 and older, went from near break-even to -15. “We have a segregated happiness society,” Peltzman told Fortune . “I can’t see that persisting without consequences.” The zeitgeist found its way recently onto Saturday Night Live . On the Nov. 14 episode, host John Mulaney played a hippie at Woodstock in 1969, laying out his generation’s plans for later life. “Hey, when we get older, I think we should buy all the houses,” he says, and then floats skipping the dying part altogether. His fellow boomers didn’t seem to understand what lay ahead in their future. Later in the show came “Sister,” a fake ad for a service in which grown brothers hand over caregiving duties for their aging fathers to their sisters, who quit their jobs and move across the country to do it. Neither sketch is about demographics, but both run on it. A generation of 76 million set the terms of every market it entered: marriage in the 1970s, then housing, and now care, as the bulge reaches the years when it needs looking after — the pig is slowly exiting the python. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

The unmarried, about 45% of adults 25 and older, went from near break-even to -15. “We have a segregated happiness society,” Peltzman told Fortune . “I can’t see that persisting without consequences.” The zeitgeist found its way recently onto Saturday Night Live . On the Nov. 14 episode, host John Mulaney played a hippie at Woodstock in 1969, laying out his generation’s plans for later life. “Hey, when we get older, I think we should buy all the houses,” he says, and then floats skipping the dying part altogether. His fellow boomers didn’t seem to understand what lay ahead in their future. Later in the show came “Sister,” a fake ad for a service in which grown brothers hand over caregiving duties for their aging fathers to their sisters, who quit their jobs and move across the country to do it. Neither sketch is about demographics, but both run on it. A generation of 76 million set the terms of every market it entered: marriage in the 1970s, then housing, and now care, as the bulge reaches the years when it needs looking after — the pig is slowly exiting the python. title: Black Friday will put AI shopping agents to the test. Consumers aren’t buying it yet
summary: Retailers have spent the year wiring their sites for AI agents, but the holiday season is shaping up as more dress rehearsal than debut.
content: Earlier this fall Visa instructed 22 different personal AI agents to purchase three everyday items—a TV, a laptop, and a hair appliance—to see how they’d do. It was not a resounding success. Only 57% of the 15 shopping trips each agent made led to a purchase that matched the shopper’s needs or even resulted in a suggestion of something suitable. Many agents misunderstood consumers’ preferences or didn’t know what questions to ask, such as, “Is this TV game-compatible?” leading to many wrong purchases. The biggest names in retail have spent the year wiring their stores and websites for AI assistants, betting shoppers will soon rely on bots for their buying. Walmart made a big show of supporting agentic commerce early this year when it announced a partnership with Google and its Gemini artificial intelligence assistant to make it easier for shoppers to discover and buy items from the world’s biggest retailer. Target consumers using ChatGPT can now tag the assistant and describe an occasion they are shopping for and get back product ideas they can buy in a single checkout. Home Depot in August expanded its AI-powered shopping assistant, Magic Apron, to all of its stores after an initial limited trial. And earlier this month, OpenAI unveiled its “Wallet” that connects with American Express , Visa and Mastercard to allow agents to pay and close out a transaction based on the limits a human customer sets. But the Visa simulation illustrates the progress agentic commerce has made and how far it still has to go. This Black Friday-to-Cyber Monday weekend gives AI shopping agents their biggest stage yet, but the holiday season won’t belong to them. Instead, the 2026 holiday shopping season will be more dress rehearsal than debut. With the National Retail Federation forecasting more than $1 trillion in total holiday sales, retailers will be watching whether shoppers rely on AI just for gift suggestions—or whether they let bots do the buying. Small numbers, big bets Agentic commerce is already showing promise for retailers who want to get ready for what they see as the technology’s inevitable rise. A report by consulting firm Kearney noted that Amazon’s AI shopping assistant supported $12 billion in incremental sales last year, or 2% of total business, and Walmart earlier in 2026 reported that users of its Sparky assistant spent 35% more per order than the average customer. Emarketer research found that in the first quarter of 2026, AI-referred traffic to U.S. retail sites rose 393% on a year-over-year basis from an admittedly small base . A Bain & Co. analysis this month of Similarweb data found that AI assistants account for less than 1% of retailers’ web traffic. Still, retail executives aren’t waiting for these teeny numbers to grow before they start placing bets. Target CEO Michael Fiddelke told Wall Street analysts last week that agentic shopping was still behind only a small amount of sales, but that “it’s important for us to be at the forefront of any changes to the consumer purchase funnel.” Meanwhile, last month, Kohl’s CEO Michael Bender said that agentic commerce was still small but drew shoppers who spent more than average, and crucially he said he saw big opportunities for “purchase confidence” to increase over time. “We have an opportunity to participate in a larger pie. And our only question is: Which are going to be the best tools to partner with and how do we make sure it doesn’t add more friction?” said Macy’s CEO Tony Spring at the Fortune Innovation Forum in Detroit earlier this month. Cool, you go first Consumers are more cautious than retail CEOs. They are still getting used to the technology and seeing what it is capable of, and, importantly, what they can count on it for. A Morning Consult poll for Visa last month found that 54% of adults had already used AI for at least one shopping task, up from 47% last year. But only 23% of U.S. consumers trust generative AI to handle payment transactions on their behalf. That finding harkens back to the hesitancy consumers first exhibited towards e-commerce and mobile commerce. That caution faded with experience and time and as mobile payment platforms proved they were reliable. Now most consumers don’t think twice about paying for things online. For now, consumers are most comfortable using AI for search, and that too poses an opportunity. “Generative AI, more than agentic commerce, will play a significant role in this year’s holiday shopping,” says Anna Marrs, group president for global Merchant & Network Services at American Express. “Consumers are using large language model tools to do a better job searching for what they want.” The limitations of retailers’ sites themselves offer an opening for AI, says Forrester Research principal analyst Emily Pfeiffer. “Retailers’ websites are terrible at comparison shopping and surfacing things you haven’t thought of before,” she said. That is especially crucial for things like gift ideas or areas where a customer is less knowledgeable. “We’re more open to suggestions,” Pfeiffer said. Crate & Barrel Holdings CEO Janet Hayes says her customers are most willing to engage with agentic commerce when they’re building wedding registries. “When it’s complex and hard and they’ve never done it, they want suggestions,” she said. “The more they ask in there, the more it informs how to write better copy and give better content.” The option to search with natural language (“a hard-shell suitcase that meets Delta Air Lines’ carry-on size requirements and costs between $100 and $200”), versus clunky key terms (“hardshell+suitcase+small”), is also an advantage of AI. “[That] will make a huge difference,” says Pfeiffer. Her research found that 20% of shoppers will flat out refuse to shop on a website that can’t handle natural language. Black Friday and the holiday season may also not be the right use case for agentic shopping. An American Express survey found that 52% of U.S. consumers are fine allowing an AI agent to purchase low-cost items like household essentials and groceries, but only 15% feel that way for big-ticket items, like electronics and appliances. And a poll this month by marketing platform provider Zeta found that only 9% of respondents would let AI purchase gifts without personally reviewing them first. Growing at the speed of trust Moving consumers’ AI use from searching and browsing to full-fledged buying requires giving them peace of mind. “Consumers need to know what’s going to happen if something goes wrong. They’re going to feel good if they know they’re going to be taken care of if an agent makes a mistake,” says Kearney partner Katherine Black, who leads the firm’s food, drug and mass market retail practice. (Walmart said in October that its returns policy applies even when an AI messes up. “Customers are in control,” Walmart wrote in a blog post .) Retailers are looking for reassurance too. They seem to love the added traffic to their sites from AI agents but also fear loss of control of the customer experience and of customer data, which supports marketing and loyalty programs. In September, Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse agent from shopping on Amazon. (Walmart is taking a different tack: last month it rolled out infrastructure to enable third-party agentic commerce by creating a profile for agents that links to a shopper’s Walmart account.) The major credit card issuers have all unveiled technology this year that allows verified AI shopping agents to make transactions with all the protections consumers are used to. Amex has announced that it plans to launch its Amex Agent Purchase Protection offer to protect eligible customers from charges when a registered AI agent makes a purchase inconsistent with the customer’s authenticated instructions. If the 2026 holiday season experiment with agentic shopping is a success, then next year’s may well prove to be the tipping point for the tech. “It’s really going to grow at the speed of trust,” says Marrs. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

title: For banks, a breach is now a matter of when, not if, says OCBC’s tech head—and reaction time matters as much as prevention
summary: For banks, trust may now come not from preventing any and all attacks, but from detecting, closing and repairing them faster.
content: Since September, South Korea’s financial sector has been hit by a rolling wave of cyberattacks , with regulators counting 40 incidents at 37 financial firms, including banks, brokerages, insurers, savings banks and crypto exchanges. Researchers traced the September attacks to Artex, an AI-powered tool that automated the intrusions. “With the velocity that cyberattacks are happening, it is a matter of when rather than if,” Praveen Raina, head of group operations and technology at Singapore’s Oversea-Chinese Banking Corp. (OCBC), tells Fortune . For banks, trust may now come not from preventing any and all attacks, but from detecting, closing and repairing them faster. “I wish I could prevent them—and we’ll try—but what we can control is having the right processes so that we can react quickly to whatever happens,” Raina says. His strategy consists of two elements: cybersecurity and resilience. “We’re leveraging AI for cybersecurity,” he explains. “With agentic AI attacking organizations, humans cannot keep up with it… it’s the nature of the beast. So, we’re building a defensive AI wrapper around the bank to protect it.” His team also regularly conducts red-teaming exercises : structured simulations in which a group acts like a real-world attacker to improve their ability to react in the event of a hack. “We practice a lot among ourselves and with other industry players,” Raina says. “We also have a bug bounty program for white hackers to identify [security] issues in exchange for a reward.” Building in-house Raina joined OCBC in 2008 as its SVP in group operations and technology , after spending the early years of his career as an IT consultant to telcos and enterprise software firms in Canada. (OCBC was founded in 1932; Today, it is Singapore’s second-largest bank, and ranks No. 13 on Fortune ’s Southeast Asia 500 list.) In his first year at OCBC, while spending the holidays away from home, Raina amassed a small team to build an iPhone-native banking app. “The tech team was a lot smaller then,” he says. “We didn’t have a deep expertise in building things, and instead mostly bought [our tech solutions] from vendors and implemented them. As the world changed around us, we made it a point [to develop in-house expertise].” (The final product, launched in 2008, was the first digital banking app debuted by one of Singapore’s three local banks: OCBC, DBS and UOB.) From then on, Raina’s team—which today consists of roughly 600 to 700 employees—started building almost everything in-house. “It gives us better control of things, and we can do more and faster releases,” he explains, adding that failing “over and over again” adds to the joy of creation. In July, OCBC launched its Avatar Banking app , which allows clients round-the-clock access to AI-enabled virtual relationship managers. The entire process from ideation to release took four to six weeks, Raina says. “It was an unplanned pregnancy,” he says. “We just happily stumbled upon the idea, and worked every day to generate ideas to see what we could do [to bring it to life].” The new app was initially launched as a beta version to just fifty customers, but Raina says he’s preparing to onboard all the bank’s private wealth clients onto the platform by the first quarter of 2027. (On the app, users can pick between two virtual wealth managers: a man named Wayne and a woman named Wendy.) “The white glove service is always important, and we are not taking that away,” says Raina, who also heads up the tech division at the Bank of Singapore, OCBC’s private banking subsidiary. “The point is, if I wake up at 3 a.m. and want to look at what’s happening with my portfolio, who do I go to? At that time, even if you call your relationship manager, they will likely not pick up.” The quantum frontier Experts estimate that “Q-Day”, the day quantum computers will be able to crack traditional encryption, will happen around the year 2030 . Raina expects a Y2K-style crunch, with every institution competing for the same vendors at the last minute. OCBC is trying to get ahead by training over 100 quantum-literate staff, and running pilots with universities and ST Engineering. “When we go into our mobile banking app, our phone sends a signal to the OCBC data center, and there’s a handshake happening and a key is exchanged to verify our identity,” Raina explains. “The issue with quantum computing is that it’s so powerful that it can break those keys… so the security layer is gone.” Raina compares quantum technology today to AI in the pre-ChatGPT era. “It’s a theoretical field, which we aren’t experts in, so we partner with universities to get a better understanding of the technology stack,” he says. “We are building [quantum security] for the future; we don’t need it today, but when the technology comes to life on Q-Day, we will be ready.” Ultimately, banking is a trust-based business, and Raina sees it as his role to upkeep the faith that users have in OCBC. “People work and they put their life savings with the organization—there’s no bigger trust than that,” he concludes. “We as an organization have to do our part to ensure that everything is protected.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

title: A study of 22,894 Oura Ring wearers ties erratic sleep times to depression and anxiety. Its author offers a simple solution
summary: UCSF and UC San Diego researchers analyzed an average of 154 days of Oura Ring data per person. Lower sleep-regularity scores tracked with worse depression, anxiety, and loneliness.
content: How long you sleep is only part of the picture. In a study of 22,894 adults who wore Oura smart rings for an average of 154 days, people whose bedtimes and wake times shifted from day to day reported more severe depression, anxiety, and loneliness, and the link held after researchers accounted for how long people slept. The research, led by UC San Francisco and UC San Diego and published Nov. 12 in Scientific Reports , measured consistency with the Sleep Regularity Index (SRI) , a 0-to-100 score. A score of 100 means someone falls asleep and wakes up at identical times every day; lower scores mean more drift. Sleep trouble is common. In 2020, 14.5% of U.S. adults had trouble falling asleep most days or every day, and 17.8% had trouble staying asleep, according to the CDC. Most advice for them centers on duration and habits, from the best sleeping position to a consistent bedtime routine . The findings also come as sleep tracking turns into big business. Oura, whose rings supplied the data and which helped fund the study, put its planned IPO on hold this fall ; at the top of its proposed range, the offering would have valued the company at $15.6 billion. Why months of data beat a single week Participants took part in TemPredict, a study launched in 2020 that used smart-ring sleep and movement data synced to the Oura app. They also completed monthly surveys on depression, anxiety, and loneliness. Researchers compared the full multi-month record against a seven-day “Typical Week” snapshot, the window most earlier sleep-regularity studies relied on. Both approaches pointed the same way, but the longer data showed stronger links to mental health. An irregular sleeper’s single week might happen to catch an unusually steady stretch. “We capture the ups and the downs, the harder weeks and the easier weeks, and we obtain a more complete picture of what someone’s sleep looks like over time,” said Ashley Mason, the study’s senior author and an associate professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at UCSF. “Short-term tracking may underestimate—but may overestimate—irregular sleep, depending on when you capture it.” Longer tracking, Mason said, can “minimize the impact that unrepresentative weeks have on a dataset.” She pointed to a UK Biobank analysis of nearly 80,000 participants that relied on one week of wrist-worn sleep data. Shyamal Patel, Oura’s senior vice president of science, said the signal from longer tracking was stronger than in a “typical week” snapshot, “which is how much shorter past studies measured sleep regularity. That’s exactly how Oura can support researchers–by making sleep-wake patterns measurable in everyday life over time, especially when paired with repeated assessments of mood and symptoms. Then, randomized interventions can test whether changing sleep routines changes outcomes.” What the numbers show According to first author Severine Soltani, an SRI of 84 corresponds to going to bed and waking up roughly an hour earlier or later than the day before, on average. At 75, that shift is closer to an hour and a half. Scores tracked symptom severity. Participants with severe depression averaged an SRI of 74.93, compared with 83.74 for those within normal limits. For severe anxiety, the average was 78.94, versus 83.67. Each 5-point drop in SRI was associated with roughly 1.5 times higher odds of severe depression. That association held after the researchers adjusted for age, sex, and average sleep duration. Mason calls the findings “correlational in nature.” She pointed to a JAMA Psychiatry study published in February, which found that irregular sleep predicted depressive relapse among adults in remission, as evidence that prioritizing regular sleep may lower the risk of declining mental health. “Sleep irregularity most likely harms mental health through circadian misalignment and its downstream effects—on hormones, inflammation, neurotransmitters, emotion regulation, and our social lives,” Mason said. “When we support circadian rhythms, we support other bodily functions.” The loneliness link Participants who reported elevated loneliness averaged an SRI of 81.79, compared with 83.75 for those within normal limits. The authors noted that sleep-regularity research has paid little attention to loneliness, despite its toll on mental health. Mason said her team approached loneliness with an “exploratory mindset” because the connection “hasn’t been studied before.” The result made sense to her once she thought about everyday routines. “If you have a morning workout class that you always go to and see friends at, you are more likely to have a regular time you wake up in order to get to the class,” she said. “Sleep regularity may be associated with other types of schedule regularity that involve social interactions.” Who funded the study, and what it can’t prove The analysis is cross-sectional, and symptoms were self-reported, so it can’t show that irregular sleep causes depression or the reverse. The study notes that participants were disproportionately white, middle-aged, and living in North America and Europe. Because the study began during the COVID-19 pandemic, the researchers focused on main sleep episodes, excluded shift workers, and did not control for factors such as living alone or individual chronotypes. Funding came from the U.S. Department of Defense, the #StartSmall Foundation, and Oura Health Oy. Mason has been paid for consulting work for Oura, and co-author Benjamin Smarr of UC San Diego has been paid for consulting work and holds a financial interest in the company. What to do with it Asked whether Oura plans to turn SRI into real-time guidance, Patel pointed to features the company already offers: Bedtime Guidance and Chronotype , “which together evaluate a user’s circadian rhythm, and provide a personalized bedtime window that appears an hour before it begins.” A Body Clock graph compares members’ recent sleep with their optimal window. Patel said Oura focuses on “giving members perspective rather than fueling fixation.” “We don’t think perfect sleep is the goal. A consistent routine that fits someone’s life is more realistic and easier to keep up,” he said. “We want members to understand their bodies with more confidence, so they can live their fullest and most vibrant life, not spend their time chasing scores.” Mason’s advice requires no device. “We cannot wave a magic wand and make ourselves fall asleep at the same time every day, but we can set an alarm clock and make ourselves wake up at the same time every day,” she said. “If you wake up at the same time every day that ends in D-A-Y (Monday, Saturday, Sunday, Tuesday, and so on), you will start to get sleepy at the same time each night, and your bedtime will regularize.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

title: Kevin O’Leary told Gen Z to invest 15% of each paycheck. One worker asked why investors get the profits
summary: In a Jubilee debate, a software engineer pressed the Shark Tank investor on equity at Starbucks and Amazon.
content: Shark Tank investor Kevin O’Leary rehashed a familiar pitch for Americans who want to get rich: spend less, save 15% of every paycheck, and let the gains compound in the stock market. But when O’Leary faced down 20 Gen Z workers in a Jubilee Media-hosted debate, one participant challenged the traditional bargain between labor and capital. Why should employees spend their lives drawing wages while investors get rich off the surplus value they create? “Why should all the money we make doing our work, our labor, why should it go to people like you? We did the work,” the participant, a software engineer named Joe, said to O’Leary. The episode of Jubilee’s YouTube series “Surrounded,” titled “1 Millionaire Boss vs 20 Gen Z Workers,” posted Nov. 15 and put the multimillionaire investor face-to-face with younger workers questioning the rules of the modern economy. The 8-minute exchange over whether workers deserve a bigger piece of the profits they help generate became one of the flashpoints of the nearly two-hour debate. The argument lands as employee ownership gets a mainstream hearing. SpaceX’s June IPO was expected to make more than 4,400 current and former employees millionaires, welders among them . And Mark Cuban has proposed that companies choose between giving every employee stock and paying higher corporate taxes . From Starbucks dividends to Amazon stock grants Joe opened with a Starbucks hypothetical: Why shouldn’t some of the chain’s billions in profits go to the workers making and serving the coffee? O’Leary argued that would shortchange investors who supplied the capital. Joe wasn’t suggesting workers get all the profits, just a bigger share. He pointed to Starbucks’ dividend payments to shareholders as evidence that the company already distributes its profits. Starbucks, which reported $37.9 billion in revenue for the fiscal year that ended Sept. 27, recently raised its dividend. The debate then moved from coffee shops to one of the country’s biggest employers: Amazon, which this year unseated Walmart as No. 1 on the 2026 Fortune 500 . Joe argued that the company offers one of the starkest examples of how pay can split by role. A software engineer with the same ability to execute and work hard as a warehouse employee could potentially receive substantial restricted stock units, or RSUs, as part of their compensation. The warehouse worker, meanwhile, might receive no equity stake, despite long shifts doing physically arduous work. Why, Joe wanted to know, should one employee have a chance to build wealth through company stock while another is limited to a paycheck? O’Leary said the labor market ultimately shapes compensation. If Amazon couldn’t find enough people willing to work in its warehouses, he said, the company would have to increase compensation to attract them. He also questioned whether equity could realistically be distributed across every type of business. “You can’t do that in every business. You can’t give equity to a utility,” O’Leary said. Joe said equity wasn’t the only answer. Companies could also offer dividends or profit-sharing arrangements that give employees a direct financial stake in their success. He pointed to O’Leary’s fellow Shark Tank investor, Mark Cuban, who gave employees equity at companies he founded and has urged every CEO to do the same. If investors can benefit financially when a business grows or is sold, Joe argued, employees who helped create that value should have a chance to benefit, too. The two did find one patch of common ground: SpaceX, where rank-and-file employees became millionaires when the company’s shares took off. O’Leary said he was perfectly fine with that outcome. Joe’s point, however, was that such windfalls are the exception, not the norm. The economy, as structured, funnels the gains from workers’ labor upward while asking employees to build wealth out of whatever is left of their paychecks. What investors bring to the table O’Leary wasn’t particularly receptive to the idea that investors were simply getting rich off other people’s labor. “I worked pretty damn hard to get rich. Really hard,” he said. Joe said that while O’Leary may have worked hard to build his fortune, he questioned what investors contribute beyond their money. O’Leary explained that he looks for entrepreneurs with promising ideas and business plans, then puts his own capital behind them. When Joe asked what he brought to the table, O’Leary answered bluntly. “Money.” The 15% rule meets the rent The exchange eventually circled back to O’Leary’s familiar advice about personal financial discipline. Rather than waiting for companies to distribute profits, he suggested workers take 15% of their weekly earnings and invest it in the stock market. O’Leary has repeatedly offered this advice to younger Americans. The investor has argued that someone earning $68,000 a year could retire a millionaire by consistently investing 15% of their income over a career. But Joe questioned how realistic that prescription was for people already struggling to cover everyday expenses. Earlier in the episode, another participant, a security guard named Kieran, described working 80 hours a week only to spend 55% of his income on rent. O’Leary said people could cut unnecessary purchases from their budgets. Joe pushed back, joking that O’Leary wouldn’t find much to criticize in his own winnowed-down wardrobe. The exchange ended on an unexpected note of encouragement. Apparently impressed by the passion of Joe’s argument, O’Leary told him he’d make “good television” and invited him to come on Shark Tank. Joe declined. “I never will,” he said. “I don’t want to be an entrepreneur, bro. I just want to live.” For a generation staring down rent, gas prices and student loans, that may be the more radical ask. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

title: Kevin O’Leary told Gen Z to invest 15% of each paycheck. One worker asked why investors get the profits
summary: In a Jubilee debate, a software engineer pressed the Shark Tank investor on equity at Starbucks and Amazon.
content: Shark Tank investor Kevin O’Leary rehashed a familiar pitch for Americans who want to get rich: spend less, save 15% of every paycheck, and let the gains compound in the stock market. But when O’Leary faced down 20 Gen Z workers in a Jubilee Media-hosted debate, one participant challenged the traditional bargain between labor and capital. Why should employees spend their lives drawing wages while investors get rich off the surplus value they create? “Why should all the money we make doing our work, our labor, why should it go to people like you? We did the work,” the participant, a software engineer named Joe, said to O’Leary. The episode of Jubilee’s YouTube series “Surrounded,” titled “1 Millionaire Boss vs 20 Gen Z Workers,” posted Nov. 15 and put the multimillionaire investor face-to-face with younger workers questioning the rules of the modern economy. The 8-minute exchange over whether workers deserve a bigger piece of the profits they help generate became one of the flashpoints of the nearly two-hour debate. The argument lands as employee ownership gets a mainstream hearing. SpaceX’s June IPO was expected to make more than 4,400 current and former employees millionaires, welders among them . And Mark Cuban has proposed that companies choose between giving every employee stock and paying higher corporate taxes . From Starbucks dividends to Amazon stock grants Joe opened with a Starbucks hypothetical: Why shouldn’t some of the chain’s billions in profits go to the workers making and serving the coffee? O’Leary argued that would shortchange investors who supplied the capital. Joe wasn’t suggesting workers get all the profits, just a bigger share. He pointed to Starbucks’ dividend payments to shareholders as evidence that the company already distributes its profits. Starbucks, which reported $37.9 billion in revenue for the fiscal year that ended Sept. 27, recently raised its dividend. The debate then moved from coffee shops to one of the country’s biggest employers: Amazon, which this year unseated Walmart as No. 1 on the 2026 Fortune 500 . Joe argued that the company offers one of the starkest examples of how pay can split by role. A software engineer with the same ability to execute and work hard as a warehouse employee could potentially receive substantial restricted stock units, or RSUs, as part of their compensation. The warehouse worker, meanwhile, might receive no equity stake, despite long shifts doing physically arduous work. Why, Joe wanted to know, should one employee have a chance to build wealth through company stock while another is limited to a paycheck? O’Leary said the labor market ultimately shapes compensation. If Amazon couldn’t find enough people willing to work in its warehouses, he said, the company would have to increase compensation to attract them. He also questioned whether equity could realistically be distributed across every type of business. “You can’t do that in every business. You can’t give equity to a utility,” O’Leary said. Joe said equity wasn’t the only answer. Companies could also offer dividends or profit-sharing arrangements that give employees a direct financial stake in their success. He pointed to O’Leary’s fellow Shark Tank investor, Mark Cuban, who gave employees equity at companies he founded and has urged every CEO to do the same. If investors can benefit financially when a business grows or is sold, Joe argued, employees who helped create that value should have a chance to benefit, too. The two did find one patch of common ground: SpaceX, where rank-and-file employees became millionaires when the company’s shares took off. O’Leary said he was perfectly fine with that outcome. Joe’s point, however, was that such windfalls are the exception, not the norm. The economy, as structured, funnels the gains from workers’ labor upward while asking employees to build wealth out of whatever is left of their paychecks. What investors bring to the table O’Leary wasn’t particularly receptive to the idea that investors were simply getting rich off other people’s labor. “I worked pretty damn hard to get rich. Really hard,” he said. Joe said that while O’Leary may have worked hard to build his fortune, he questioned what investors contribute beyond their money. O’Leary explained that he looks for entrepreneurs with promising ideas and business plans, then puts his own capital behind them. When Joe asked what he brought to the table, O’Leary answered bluntly. “Money.” The 15% rule meets the rent The exchange eventually circled back to O’Leary’s familiar advice about personal financial discipline. Rather than waiting for companies to distribute profits, he suggested workers take 15% of their weekly earnings and invest it in the stock market. O’Leary has repeatedly offered this advice to younger Americans. The investor has argued that someone earning $68,000 a year could retire a millionaire by consistently investing 15% of their income over a career. But Joe questioned how realistic that prescription was for people already struggling to cover everyday expenses. Earlier in the episode, another participant, a security guard named Kieran, described working 80 hours a week only to spend 55% of his income on rent. O’Leary said people could cut unnecessary purchases from their budgets. Joe pushed back, joking that O’Leary wouldn’t find much to criticize in his own winnowed-down wardrobe. The exchange ended on an unexpected note of encouragement. Apparently impressed by the passion of Joe’s argument, O’Leary told him he’d make “good television” and invited him to come on Shark Tank. Joe declined. “I never will,” he said. “I don’t want to be an entrepreneur, bro. I just want to live.” For a generation staring down rent, gas prices and student loans, that may be the more radical ask. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

title: ‘They’ll all go to Florida’: New IRS data reignites the fight over Massachusetts’ millionaires tax
summary: Filers earning $200,000 or more drove 64% of the income loss, per the Pioneer Institute. The 4% surtax still brought in a record $3.38 billion in fiscal 2026.
content: New IRS figures may offer the clearest picture yet of how Massachusetts’ surtax on high-income residents is shaping the state’s population—and the tax base the ballot measure sought to tap. Massachusetts lost a net 31,384 residents to other states and countries between 2023 and 2024, according to IRS data reported by Boston.com . Those departing households took $3.64 billion in adjusted gross income with them. The net migration loss was slightly larger than the year before, though the income loss shrank from $4.18 billion. The numbers arrive nearly four years after the so-called “millionaires tax”—a 4% surcharge on annual income above roughly $1.1 million, indexed to inflation—took effect to fund schools and transportation. The figures capture moves, not their motives . Still, they are fuel for a perpetual debate: Do taxes on high earners drive wealthy households away, undermining the revenue they were meant to raise? New Hampshire and Florida absorb the biggest share Departing residents have clear destinations. New Hampshire gained a net 7,818 residents from Massachusetts, while Florida picked up 6,032. Together, those two states accounted for roughly 44% of Massachusetts’ net migration loss. The money followed the same routes. Massachusetts lost a net $1.29 billion in adjusted gross income to Florida and $869 million to New Hampshire, together about 59% of the state’s total. Neither destination has a state income tax. Each of Massachusetts’ New England neighbors—New Hampshire, Maine, Rhode Island, Connecticut, and Vermont—also gained more residents from the Bay State than it sent back. Young professionals and high earners drove much of the loss, according to an analysis of the IRS data by the Pioneer Institute, a Boston-based think tank. Tax filers ages 26 to 34 made up 43% of the state’s net loss of filers in 2024, and those earning $200,000 or more accounted for $2.32 billion, or 64%, of the net income loss. The IRS tracks migration by comparing addresses on consecutive years’ tax returns, capturing both the number of people on those returns and their adjusted gross income. The traffic ran both ways. New York sent the most newcomers to Massachusetts (13,394), followed by Florida (11,728) and California (8,728). Massachusetts also led its exchanges with a handful of states, with a net gain of 855 residents from New Jersey, plus smaller gains from Louisiana and Indiana. The surtax keeps beating its forecasts Whatever the migration data show, the tax itself has not come up short. The Massachusetts Department of Revenue preliminarily certified $3.38 billion in surtax collections for fiscal 2026 , a record, and well above the $2.4 billion the state budget had assumed . That compares with roughly $3 billion in fiscal 2025 and the $1.8 billion the state reported in May 2024, double what officials expected . Supporters and critics read the same numbers differently. After the IRS’s March release, MassBudget, a Boston-based research group, argued the data showed affordability, not taxes, driving the state’s out-migration . Other states are moving in Massachusetts’ direction regardless. Washington voters on Nov. 3 kept a new 9.9% tax on income above $1 million, and two of the neighbors now gaining Bay Staters, Maine and Rhode Island, enacted their own surcharges on millionaire income this year . An income tax is not a wealth tax The Massachusetts data lands amid a broader debate over whether governments can tax high earners and wealthy households without prompting them to move. But the policies under scrutiny aren’t all the same. Massachusetts’ millionaires tax is an income tax surcharge: It adds 4 percentage points to the state income tax on annual income above the threshold. California’s Proposition 40, which voters rejected on Nov. 3, targeted wealth itself, with a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the state’s roughly 200 billionaires. A wealth tax can apply even when assets are “unrealized,” meaning they haven’t been sold or generated taxable income. Peter Barnes, a former U.S. deputy international tax counsel and longtime General Electric tax lawyer, said the history of wealth taxes abroad warns states attempting them on their own. He noted that France saw flight from its wealth tax and has since effectively eliminated it, replacing it in 2018 with a narrower levy on real estate. “That’s the same thing that doomed the California wealth tax—this idea that, ‘Oh my god, they’ll all go to Florida,’” Barnes said. “I think first of all, it needs to be a whole U.S. federal tax. I don’t think a state can successfully do it.” Chester Spatt, a professor of finance at Carnegie Mellon University, previously told Fortune he was skeptical that steep wealth taxes can generate the revenue their proponents expect. “It would indirectly represent a very heavy tax on investment income,” Spatt said. “I suspect it won’t raise much revenue and instead lead to the development of devices that would be outside the reach of the tax.” For now, Massachusetts remains a laboratory of democracy—testing whether taxing high earners at the state level can work, or whether, as critics warn, it simply accelerates their departure. title: Black and Latino workers are about 20% likelier than White workers to need a new career by 2035 as AI reshapes work, McKinsey says
summary: McKinsey projects AI could eliminate more of the work in jobs Black and Latino workers hold, and fewer have a clear path out.
content: Black and Latino workers are about 20% more likely than White workers to need to move into an entirely new occupation by 2035 as AI and automation reshape work, according to projections in a new report from the McKinsey Institute for Economic Mobility released Nov. 20. AI and automation could take over about the same share of work across racial groups, McKinsey projects. What differs is whether that work disappears. McKinsey estimates that automation could reduce an average of 21% of current U.S. work hours by 2035. Of the hours it takes over, 40% of those worked by Black workers and 41% of those worked by Latino workers would be displaced, compared with 37% for White workers and 36% for Asian workers, meaning employers would need fewer people, rather than an augmented environment in which the technology supports a person doing the job. The report ties the gap to the kinds of jobs people hold. Automation is most likely to replace tasks that are standardized, easy to check and low-stakes when wrong. McKinsey’s example is answering a routine billing question, as opposed to adjusting a patient’s medication dose. Tasks like the billing question make up a larger share of the hours Black and Latino workers put in. Physical work, which is increasingly exposed to robotics, accounts for 35% of Black workers’ hours and 39% of Latino workers’ hours, compared with 26% for White workers. The jobs most exposed to AI are predominantly held by Black and Latino workers. McKinsey Report “Our research indicates that while AI and automation are expected to affect a similar share of work hours across racial groups, the consequences may differ significantly,” Duwain Pinder, a partner at McKinsey & Company, said to Fortune in a statement. “While displacement doesn’t vary significantly between cognitive and physical work, the central question is not only how much work AI and automation technologies can perform, but whose work it replaces and through which types of activities.” The effects are projected to concentrate in specific jobs: Black workers hold more than their share of the workforce in each of the six occupations with the steepest projected declines in labor demand. Latino workers hold 43% of hand packer and packager jobs, 2.3 times their share of the workforce. The differences carry into projected job growth. Based on today’s jobs, McKinsey projects total work hours for Latino workers will grow 1.4% between 2025 and 2035 and 2.1% for Black workers. For White workers, it projects 3.4%, and for Asian workers, 5.8%. The report builds on the McKinsey Global Institute’s “Workforce in motion” study , which found that automation could cut demand for about 36 million U.S. jobs by 2035 while growth elsewhere adds about 41 million. About 11 million workers may need to move into entirely different occupations. Lower-wage workers are 7.6 times as likely as higher-wage workers to be among them. Only about 14% of workers who may need to switch have a direct path into a growing job, meaning minimal retraining and no pay cut. Among workers earning less than $38,000 a year, about 10% do, compared with almost 40% of workers in the top wage bracket. Private AI investment reached nearly $345 billion globally in 2025, according to Stanford’s AI Index, which the report cites. McKinsey finds White workers are 30% to 50% more likely than Black and Latino workers to work in the areas where it expects that capital, and the jobs and wealth that come with it, to concentrate over the next two decades, including AI software, semiconductors, robotics and biotech. The report also points to strain on new workers more broadly. It cites Stanford’s tracking of young workers , which found that employment for 22- to 25-year-olds in some highly AI-exposed jobs is 19% lower than it would be had it kept pace with less-exposed jobs. McKinsey flags risks that could make the gaps worse. About one in six U.S. households has no internet connection, and Black adults are roughly 80% to 90% more likely than White adults to lack broadband. A Stanford study of 4 million job applications cited in the report found that 26% of Black applicants applied to jobs where an AI hiring tool discriminated against their group. The report also argues AI could help at key points in people’s lives. It cites an AI model built on data from Medicaid-enrolled women that flagged pregnancy risks a median of 55 days before standard clinical signs. Simulations projected up to a 31.8% drop in adverse outcomes. On schools, it notes the evidence is mixed and points to New York City’s one-year ban on student-facing AI for pre-K through eighth grade. This is not the first time McKinsey has warned that AI could deepen racial gaps. In 2023, it estimated that generative AI could widen the wealth gap between Black and White households by $43 billion a year by 2045. The new report calls on employers to train frontline workers in AI and hire on skills rather than degrees. It asks investors to require bias testing of AI tools broken out by race, income and geography. It also urges states to use federal broadband funds to reach communities that are still offline. title: Mike Cannon-Brookes on the string of accidents that created $35 billion Atlassian: ‘Don’t copy our story … It’s not a model for how to do things’
summary: He sent an email to classmates asking if “there's anyone who kind of does not want to get a real job” and whether they wanted to start a new company—with no idea of what that company might be.
content: Today, the enterprise software company Atlassian has a market cap of $35 billion, a revenue run-rate of $8 billion, and 13,000-plus employees worldwide. CEO Mike Cannon-Brookes has a personal net worth of $10 billion, because his ownership of the company was never diluted by VC money when the company was a brand-new startup. But the funny thing about the origins of Atlassian, back in the early 2000s, is that the company formed largely based on a series of accidents, Cannon-Brookes told Fortune . “Don’t copy our story. It’s not very good; it’s not. It’s not a model for how to do things,” he said on a lightning visit to Web Summit in Lisbon. Cannon-Brookes and cofounder Scott Farquhar took the same course at the University of New South Wales. Both had applied only for courses funded by scholarships. Cannon-Brookes originally wanted to be an architect (and jokes that he still would if he ever got the time). But the finances were not there. “Anyone that was going to give you money to go to university, I applied for all sorts of scholarships,” he said. Farquhar had also successfully applied for the Australian Defense Force Academy, but his letter of acceptance got lost in the mail. Thinking he had been rejected, he took one of the same scholarships that Cannon-Brookes had: $15,000 (Australian) per year, tax-free, to do a course that was a mix of computer studies and finance. The course came with a work-experience placement. “We would go to these companies in, like Wisconsin, for six months of installing [Microsoft] Windows” on office desktop computers. This was back in the era when updating operating software meant inserting a physical CD into the machine. “For months, Scott was upgrading Microsoft Windows 95 to Windows 98 or something,” Cannon-Brookes said. “[He] was, like, dude, this is the most boring shit ever. And I had a couple of placements that were similarly mind-numbing.” “The good part about that was, we were both really sour on corporate life.” While he was still an undergrad, Cannon-Brookes had sold a small startup named The Bookmark Box (it helped you manage your bookmarks) to Blink.com , an early web search tool company. With that project done, Cannon-Brookes was at a loose end. He sent an email to some of his classmates asking if “there’s anyone who kind of does not want to get a real job” and whether they wanted to start a new company with him—with no idea of what that company might be—“and Scott was the only person in the three or four that replied.” “And so he’s like, ‘I’m in.’ And so we went ‘Great. We’ll start a business. What should we do?’ Which is the worst way to start a business.” They first planned to work with customer support teams. They grew unhappy with their bug-tracking software, so they built their own. That became Jira, Atlassian’s flagship project and issue tracking tool. Next came the problem of how to sell it. They had a website with a downloadable Word document that customers could fill out with their credit card details, print, and then fax to Atlassian, where Cannon-Brookes and Farquhar would then physically punch the order into their own PC to process the payment. They did this for more than two years. At the time, roughly 2001, the vast majority of software sold over the internet was on DVDs because the internet was delivered on telephone lines, which had extremely limited bandwidth. Cannon-Brookes said that he and his partner had two major hunches early on: “The first hunch was that the internet would be a good way to distribute enterprise software. And the second was that open-source would markedly change the ability for us to make commercial applications at an order of magnitude less price.” “And both turn out to be quite spectacularly correct hunches,” he said. title: Shoppers helped pay Trump’s tariffs. Now Target, Best Buy, and Kohl’s are booking $387 million in refunds
summary: The three retailers booked $387 million in refund benefits last quarter, while Walmart and Target say they're cutting prices rather than paying shoppers back.
content: American consumers helped foot the bill for President Donald Trump’s tariffs as retailers passed higher import costs on through price increases. Now the refunds are flowing back, and they are showing up in retailers’ profits rather than in shoppers’ bank accounts. Best Buy and Kohl’s both reported better-than-expected quarterly results on Tuesday, after Target beat expectations last week. Together, the three retailers recognized $387 million in tariff refund benefits in their latest quarters. The money traces back to February, when the Supreme Court ruled that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) did not authorize the president to impose tariffs, invalidating a significant portion of Trump’s tariff regime. As of Nov. 5, U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) had certified approximately $128.4 billion in tariff refunds, including interest, and sent them to the Treasury Department for payment, according to a Nov. 10 filing with the U.S. Court of International Trade. Tariff refunds are boosting retailers’ profits Kohl’s reported third-quarter comparable sales growth of just 1.2%, yet its net income jumped to $254 million from $8 million a year earlier. Much of that came from one-time items: a $137 million tax benefit, a $61 million gain from the sale of two properties, and $45 million in tariff refund benefits, according to the company’s third-quarter earnings release . The department store chain has received approximately $190 million in tariff refunds this fiscal year. It now expects those refunds to add $1.03 to its full-year earnings per share, nearly a quarter of its raised forecast of $4.30 to $4.50. Best Buy reported comparable sales growth of 6.1%, its strongest in five years, in Jason Bonfig’s first earnings report as CEO . Net income more than doubled to $353 million from $140 million, according to the company’s earnings release . In May 2025, Best Buy’s then-CEO Corie Barry said the electronics retailer had already raised prices on some products to offset the costs of Trump’s tariffs. This quarter, the company recorded $41 million in tariff refund benefits, which helped lift profitability. Target has recognized approximately $1.3 billion in tariff refund benefits in the first nine months of its fiscal year, including $301 million in the third quarter alone. Its quarterly net income rose to $1.2 billion from $689 million, and tariff refunds accounted for $228 million of that after taxes, or nearly a fifth, according to Target’s third-quarter results . All three retailers are seeing sales rebound. But the refunds are boosting profits without requiring them to sell a single extra product. Shoppers paid a large share of the tariffs Best Buy was far from alone in passing higher import costs on to shoppers. An April analysis by Harvard Business School researchers , who tracked daily prices of nearly 360,000 products at five major U.S. retailers, estimated that consumers shouldered up to 43% of the tariff costs in the first seven months after the new tariffs were imposed. U.S. businesses absorbed the rest. Trump’s tariffs amounted to an average tax increase of $1,000 per U.S. household in 2025, according to estimates from the Tax Foundation . In February, Goldman Sachs economists estimated that tariffs had raised core PCE prices, the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation gauge, by about 0.7% through January. The effect outlasted the ruling. Researchers at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York and Columbia University estimated that consumer goods prices were still about 2% higher in August than they would have been without the tariffs imposed since early 2025. Some Americans who paid customs charges directly on overseas purchases are receiving refunds through shipping companies including FedEx , UPS , and DHL . The federal refund system offers no such relief to shoppers who paid higher prices at their local stores. Lawmakers are pressing companies to give the money back Earlier this month, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) and fellow Democratic senators asked the Federal Trade Commission to investigate whether companies that raised prices in response to tariffs and then kept the refunds violated federal law. Warren’s office accused corporations of “pocketing tariff refunds after raising prices on consumers.” The senators cited responses from five major companies: Walmart , Nike , Apple , Target, and Energizer. None committed to directly reimbursing consumers who had paid higher prices because of the tariffs. Several major companies have either ruled out direct refunds to shoppers or remained silent on the issue, as Fortune previously reported . In August, Walmart said it was using its tariff refunds to lower prices, having received nearly all of the $2.9 billion it was owed. CBS News reported that the retailer cut prices on thousands of items in July. Target is doing the same. In August, Target CFO Jim Lee said the retailer would focus on lowering prices but made no commitment to directly refunding shoppers. The retailer said last week it had lowered prices on nearly 2,000 home, apparel, and accessories products during the third quarter, on top of more than 10,000 price reductions over the past year. But lowering prices for future purchases is different from compensating customers for past ones. A shopper who paid more for a television or a piece of furniture last year may have no reason to buy another one this holiday season, even if it is now cheaper. U.S. businesses absorbed the rest. Trump’s tariffs amounted to an average tax increase of $1,000 per U.S. household in 2025, according to estimates from the Tax Foundation . In February, Goldman Sachs economists estimated that tariffs had raised core PCE prices, the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation gauge, by about 0.7% through January. The effect outlasted the ruling. Researchers at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York and Columbia University estimated that consumer goods prices were still about 2% higher in August than they would have been without the tariffs imposed since early 2025. Some Americans who paid customs charges directly on overseas purchases are receiving refunds through shipping companies including FedEx , UPS , and DHL . The federal refund system offers no such relief to shoppers who paid higher prices at their local stores. Lawmakers are pressing companies to give the money back Earlier this month, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) and fellow Democratic senators asked the Federal Trade Commission to investigate whether companies that raised prices in response to tariffs and then kept the refunds violated federal law. Warren’s office accused corporations of “pocketing tariff refunds after raising prices on consumers.” The senators cited responses from five major companies: Walmart , Nike , Apple , Target, and Energizer. None committed to directly reimbursing consumers who had paid higher prices because of the tariffs. Several major companies have either ruled out direct refunds to shoppers or remained silent on the issue, as Fortune previously reported . In August, Walmart said it was using its tariff refunds to lower prices, having received nearly all of the $2.9 billion it was owed. CBS News reported that the retailer cut prices on thousands of items in July. Target is doing the same. In August, Target CFO Jim Lee said the retailer would focus on lowering prices but made no commitment to directly refunding shoppers. The retailer said last week it had lowered prices on nearly 2,000 home, apparel, and accessories products during the third quarter, on top of more than 10,000 price reductions over the past year. But lowering prices for future purchases is different from compensating customers for past ones. A shopper who paid more for a television or a piece of furniture last year may have no reason to buy another one this holiday season, even if it is now cheaper.
